headings.title: Introduction to Joints and Articulations
headings.content: A **joint**, or articulation, is any point where two or more bones meet in the human skeleton. Without these meeting points, our skeleton would be one rigid, inflexible structure, making movement completely impossible. Joints connect hard bones together while allowing varying degrees of flexibility depending on what the body part needs to do. Some joints, like the ones between the bones of the skull, are meant to be completely fixed to protect vital organs inside. Other joints, like the knee or shoulder, are built to move freely through wide ranges of motion. Studying joints helps us understand how the muscular system pulls on the skeletal system to produce every step, reach, and turn we make every day.

headings.title: Classification of Joints: Structural and Functional
headings.content:
Nurses and doctors classify joints using two main systems: structural and functional. 

- **Structural classification**: Based on the type of tissue holding the bones together and whether there is a fluid-filled space. The categories are **fibrous joints**, **cartilaginous joints**, and **synovial joints**.
- **Functional classification**: Based on how much movement the joint allows. 
  - **Synarthrosis**: An immovable joint, such as skull sutures.
  - **Amphiarthrosis**: A slightly movable joint, such as the pubic symphysis.
  - **Diarthrosis**: A freely movable joint, such as the hip or elbow.

headings.title: Primary Function: Facilitating Body Movement
headings.content: The most visible function of joints is to allow body movement. Bones act as hard levers, and skeletal muscles provide the pulling force. When a muscle contracts, it pulls across a joint, causing the bones to pivot or rotate around that junction. The specific shape of the joint determines what kind of movements are possible. Hinge joints like the elbow allow bending and straightening in one direction, while ball-and-socket joints like the shoulder allow rotation in multiple directions. Without functional joints, coordinated physical activity and everyday tasks would come to a complete halt.

headings.title: Providing Structural Stability and Weight-Bearing
headings.content: While some joints are built for wide movement, others are designed primarily for stability and weight-bearing. Joints in the lower extremities, such as the hips, knees, and ankles, must support the entire weight of the upper body against the pull of gravity. Tough fibrous bands called **ligaments** connect bone to bone, holding the joint tightly in place to prevent abnormal twisting or dislocation. When these stabilizing structures are weakened by injury or disease, the joint becomes unstable, making it difficult for the patient to stand or walk safely.

headings.title: Role of Synovial Fluid and Cartilage in Joint Protection
headings.content: Freely movable synovial joints experience a lot of physical friction during daily use. To prevent bones from grinding against each other, the ends of the bones are covered with a smooth, slippery layer of **articular cartilage**. Surrounding the joint is a capsule filled with **synovial fluid**, a thick liquid that acts like engine oil to lubricate the surfaces, absorb shock, and supply nutrients to the cartilage. Without this natural cushioning and lubrication system, everyday movement would quickly wear down bone tissue and cause severe pain.

headings.title: Maintaining Posture and Skeletal Alignment
headings.content: Joints do more than just help us move from place to place; they also play a vital role in keeping our bodies upright and aligned. Small adjustments made across multiple joints in the spine, pelvis, and legs allow us to maintain an upright posture without constantly falling over. Small muscles surrounding these joints make micro-adjustments all day long to keep our center of gravity balanced. Good skeletal alignment reduces unnecessary strain on individual joints and prevents early fatigue in supporting muscle groups.

headings.title: Clinical Implications and Common Joint Pathologies
headings.content:
Because joints endure continuous physical stress throughout life, they are prone to various diseases and injuries. Two of the most common joint disorders seen in clinical practice are **osteoarthritis** and **rheumatoid arthritis**. 

- **Osteoarthritis**: A degenerative "wear and tear" condition where protective cartilage breaks down over time, leading to pain and stiffness.
- **Rheumatoid arthritis**: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder where the body's immune system attacks its own synovial membranes.

Nurses must assess patients for joint pain, swelling, and limited range of motion to help manage these chronic conditions effectively.
